sources.title: National Register of Historic Places listings in Buffalo, New York
Wikipedia GeoSearch, 2.5 km radius around Niagara Square (42.8864, -78.8784)

stops.name: Buffalo City Hall
stops.description: A 398 foot Art Deco tower finished in 1931, with a free observation deck on the 28th floor that looks out over the city and Lake Erie.

stops.name: McKinley Monument
stops.description: The 96 foot obelisk at the center of Niagara Square was dedicated in 1907 to William McKinley, shot six years earlier at Buffalo's Pan-American Exposition.

stops.name: Old County Hall
stops.description: Andrew Jackson Warner's granite courthouse went up between 1871 and 1875 and served as both county and city seat until Buffalo built its own hall in 1929.

stops.name: St. Paul's Episcopal Cathedral
stops.description: Richard Upjohn considered this Medina sandstone cathedral his finest work; fire gutted the interior in 1888 and Robert Gibson rebuilt it behind the surviving walls.

stops.name: Guaranty Building
stops.description: Louis Sullivan and Dankmar Adler wrapped this 1896 steel frame in ornamented terra cotta, and it is still one of the clearest statements of what an early skyscraper could look like.

stops.name: Buffalo and Erie County Naval & Military Park
stops.description: The largest inland naval park in the country, with the cruiser USS Little Rock, the destroyer USS The Sullivans and the submarine USS Croaker moored at Canalside.

stops.name: Ellicott Square Building
stops.description: When it opened in 1896 this was the largest office building in the world by floor area, and its glass roofed central court is open to walk through.

stops.name: Old Post Office
stops.description: A Gothic Revival federal post office completed in 1901, sorting mail until the 1960s and housing SUNY Erie's City Campus since 1981.

stops.name: Hotel Lafayette
stops.description: Louise Blanchard Bethune, the first American woman to practice architecture professionally, designed this French Renaissance hotel, brought back by a 35 million dollar restoration in 2012.

stops.name: Colored Musicians Club
stops.description: Founded in 1935 by the members of Buffalo's segregated Local 533, this is the last club of its kind still running, with a jazz museum on the ground floor.

stops.name: Michigan Street Baptist Church
stops.description: Built in 1845 by a congregation of freedom seekers, this Underground Railroad station reopened in January 2025 after a four year restoration of its sanctuary.

stops.name: Electric Tower
stops.description: This 1912 tower is a permanent stone answer to the temporary Electric Tower that lit up the 1901 Pan-American Exposition, and Buffalo drops its New Year's ball from it.

stops.name: Liberty Building
stops.description: Two 36 foot replicas of the Statue of Liberty stand on the roof of this 1925 tower, one facing east and one west for Buffalo's place between the coast and the lakes.

stops.name: Buffalo Savings Bank
stops.description: Green and Wicks finished this Beaux-Arts bank in 1901 under a gilded dome 56 feet across, regilded three times and visible from most of lower Main Street.

stops.name: Shea's Buffalo Theatre
stops.description: A 1926 Rapp and Rapp movie palace with interiors by Louis Comfort Tiffany, saved from demolition in the 1970s and still playing its original Wurlitzer organ.

note: Buffalo has never come up in this file's history, so it wins the rotation outright. Fifteen stops, all verified against their own Wikipedia articles, all with a street address and a looked-up ZIP. The cluster is downtown: Niagara Square, lower Main Street, the theatre district and Canalside, plus two stops on the Michigan Street African American Heritage Corridor about half a mile east. That pushes the full walk closer to a mile and a half than a mile, but the two eastern stops are the strongest history on the list and are worth the extra blocks. Address note for the human: Wikipedia's infobox for Old County Hall says 100 Franklin St, while the Erie County Clerk, which occupies the building, gives 92 Franklin St; I used 92, which is also the address buffaloah.com files it under. Guaranty Building is listed on the NRHP as 28 Church Street but its occupant's mailing address is 140 Pearl Street, the corner entrance, so I used the Pearl Street form since that is the one with a confirmed ZIP. Michigan Street Baptist Church needed an outside check: the Wikipedia article is ambiguous about whether the 1845 building survives, and local reporting confirms it reopened to the public in January 2025 after a 1.9 million dollar restoration. Dropped: Erie County Savings Bank (demolished 1968), Anchor Bar and Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site (both real and both good, but a mile or more north of the core), Buffalo Central Terminal (well outside downtown), and the Metro Rail stations, which are transit stops rather than places to stand in front of.
